rv.q: This elliptical approach is in part its strength, subtly illuminating how trying to move past one tragedy may bring a family to the precipice of another.

This disjunction between what the audience sees and what the characters see is the core mechanism of Zeldin’s beautifully directed, if underwritten, play, which (sort of) adapts Sophocles’ “Antigone” to a contemporary household.
Yet The Other Place, like many other attempts to modernize the Greeks, has a hole where the ancient gods, fates and rituals should be.
The craftwork is all topflight and probably expensive, yet it chokes the performances rather than revealing them.
Tragedy is the defining theme of the show, no less epic for its setting in a suburban home rather than a Greek palace.
Thanks to the superb performances and the playwright’s riveting staging you’re mesmerized for every one of its concise 80 minutes.
“The Other Place” is at its best an intensely acted exploration of grief and family dynamics.
It stands on its own as inspired by Antigone but fails to have the same impact both in its lack of tension and in its build up to its conclusion.
Ultimately, Zeldin's sensationalistic conclusion feels hollow: it's earnestly performed and entirely insubstantial.
Worse, when a Greek tragedy is reduced to 80 minutes (the running time here), you end up with nothing more than a tawdry soap opera.
“The Other Place” deserves the recognition it received in London.
A multisensory Greek tragedy disguised as a house renovation, The Other Place descends into family dysfunction with haunting inevitability.
This first-class production has had the smarts to bring its two leads across the pond.
Alexander Zeldin‘s The Other Place, hisses a torrent of silent shame.
The Other Place is sometimes frustrating but ultimately rewarding.
What’s missing is the organic aura of inevitability that’s integral to Sophocles’ own storytelling.
The play was written specifically for D'Arcy (House of the Dragon, Bluets), who is fearless as Annie, who resents having to return home but feels the need to protect what was hers and her father's.

cn.t: Zeldin's Antigone-inspired family drama divides critics with its naturalistic approach and emotional restraint. Performances, especially D'Arcy and Menzies, earn praise, but many find the modernization underdeveloped and motives unclear.
